Ruth Santiago’s home in southeastern Puerto Rico, in Guayama, is one of a planned 25 homes that will model how the island can revolutionize energy generation through distributed rooftop solar and battery storage. 
 
☀️The people of Guayama live with the effect of coal burning and coal-ash waste from the nearby AES coal-fired power plant there. Coal ash waste is linked to heart disease,  cancer, lung illnesses and neurological disorders. 
 
☀️But, Santiago--an environmental attorney who works with the El Puente Latino Climate Action Network—said the island’s residents don’t have to be captive to fossil fuel interests who are harming public health and contributing to global warming. 
 
☀️Instead, they can be pro-sumers, producing energy, instead of consumers. It’s what she calls energy democracy, where the people have the power instead of the polluters. 
 
☀️Now, with nonprofit funds for coal ash mitigation, the Comite Dialogo Ambiental (Environmental Dialogue Committee) a group in her area is having rooftop solar and battery storage systems installed on 25 rooftops. 
 
“The project drives home the message that clean energy generation alternatives that can be readily implemented and that coal combustion for energy production and its related residual waste can be avoided,” she said, adding: “A radical energy system transformation is doable in Puerto Rico.” 

Head over to our Stories to lean more about Ruth's work advocating for solar in Puerto Rico.	renewables

The Senate Business and Commerce Committee had a hearing with state regulators this week to get a read on their progress with Winter Storm URI legislation.

One of the things I pride is that the Senators of both parties don’t mind mixing it up with state bureaucrats when necessary if they are NOT getting the clear direction out of our legislation.

Nothing can be clearer - changes in Texas governance, procedures, reporting, preparation, and winterization must follow in the wake of Winter Storm URI. The public expects no less, and I believe we are still short several MW of thermal energy, aka, coal, gas, and nuclear electric generation plants that we'll need in Texas now and in the future.

Greg Groogan's article (https://www.fox26houston.com/news/with-winter-approaching-questions-loom-over-texas-grid-readiness) captures the frustration of several Senators as the Railroad Commission directors do not seem to get the need to proceed post haste on making sure it's clear that we need to be checking on gas pipelines and winterization efforts!

Normally, Senator Whitmire and I can be a bipartisan Q&A tag team in Senate Finance, but here, my colleague Senator Campbell steps up to ask tough questions as I'm not on this particular committee, but very proud of the points they made in the hearing!

The bottom line is what gets measured gets fixed! We know what happened in Winter Storm URI, and we're not going to let this "fix" effort drop for any reason. Watch the video and spread the word! Sen. PB. 	renewables

We are seeking to expand our public electric vehicle charger network and implement lower EV charging rates as part of our ongoing effort to help Hawaii achieve our decarbonization goals. We are asking the Public Utilities Commission (PUC) to approve our proposed Public Electric Vehicle Charger Expansion Project.
 
The proposed project is the most significant EV charging initiative undertaken by us. It builds on our experience from providing public fast charging for more than seven years under a pilot program approved by the PUC. In that time, the EV market in Hawaii has grown markedly, creating a need for more charging stations to meet demand. And every major global vehicle manufacturer, including Ford, General Motors, Volkswagen and Jaguar, have announced plans to transition a large share of their products to electric over the next decade.

If approved by the PUC, we would look to install and operate approximately 150 single-port DC fast charging stations and 150 dual-port Level 2 charging stations at roughly 75 sites across our service territory from 2023 through 2030. About 60% of the sites would be on Oahu, 20% in Maui County and 20% on Hawaii Island.
 
“Providing drivers with expanded public charging options is critical to serving more electric vehicles on Hawaii’s roadways,” said Aki Marceau, our director of electrification of transportation. “Hawaiian Electric is committed to taking action on climate change by helping to decarbonize Hawaii’s economy, and electrifying ground transportation is a major part of that effort.” Read more: http://hwnelec.co/vUhS50GCMRJ.	renewables
